title: The Breakeven Mile
primary_metric: total annual transportation cost (USD) as a linear function of annual miles driven m, for each option, compared at the breakeven mileage m* where the two lines cross

options.A: Keys of Her Own — buy the used sedan, taking on fixed loan, insurance, and registration costs every year regardless of mileage, plus a constant per-mile operating cost
options.B: The All-App Life — stay car-free, pay a flat per-mile rideshare rate for every mile driven, with zero fixed cost

reinforcement_note: Both claimed skills (statistics-and-probability-system-of-equations, statistics-and-probability-how-to-solve-a-system-of-linear-equations) carry n=2 as of 2026-09-03, confirmed live against readmodel/standards_spine.json -- thin, but not zero-coverage. This case does not close a skill-count gap; it closes the topic gap the concept sheet identified (Life-skills taxonomy cluster #3, Major purchase decisions -- car ownership vs. rideshare had zero published coverage before this case). This is the same honest framing used in cases/the-two-offers/case.json and cases/the-lease-break/case.json, both of which also disclose new_coverage: [] rather than force a false zero-coverage claim. The calculus-track version of this concept was tried first (calculus-how-to-use-the-quotient-rule-to-differentiate-a-quotient-of-functions, n=0, a genuine zero-coverage close) per the concept sheet's own recommendation, but case-research found its load-bearing premise -- a genuinely accelerating, mileage-driven depreciation-per-mile curve -- does not hold against real sourced data (see redesign_2026_09_03 and RESEARCH_LOG.md). This linear version is the concept sheet's own documented fallback.

redesign_2026_09_03.reason: case-research (run 2026-09-03) found the original calculus/quotient-rule track's load-bearing premise -- a genuinely accelerating, mileage-driven depreciation-per-mile curve -- does not hold against real sourced data. AAA 'Your Driving Costs' (fetched directly, the best available primary source) shows depreciation-per-mile FALLING as annual mileage rises ($0.3108 -> $0.2308 -> $0.1937/mi at 10k/15k/20k mi/yr, medium-sedan segment), a fixed-cost-dilution pattern consistent with a LINEAR total-cost model, not the nonlinear one the quotient-rule optimization needed. See RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full search trail (retained from the prior pass, with a new entry appended for this redesign).
redesign_2026_09_03.redesigned_to: The concept sheet's own documented fallback: the simple linear breakeven-mileage model (A: total cost = fixed costs + per-mile rate x miles; B: total cost = rideshare rate x miles; find where the two lines cross).

redesign_2026_09_03.retuned_for_balance: MA1 (Renata's own annual mileage) was revised from 11,500 mi/yr (roughly national-average scale, which produces a ~67% landslide margin under the linear model -- unbalanced per SPEC §2's 20% ceiling) down to 2,760 mi/yr, with an explicit arithmetic justification (a compact single-neighborhood route: ~10 mi/workday x 250 workdays + ~260 mi/yr errands). This is the SPEC §2-compliant move: retune a disclosed modeling assumption, not a sourced figure, and not by hiding data. At 2,760 mi/yr the margin is 11.24%, inside the concept sheet's 8-12% target.

track_decision: Concept #2 explicitly offered two tracks: a linear breakeven-mileage version (reinforcing statistics-and-probability-system-of-equations / how-to-solve-a-system-of-linear-equations, both n=2 -- thin but NOT zero) or a calculus version minimizing average cost-per-mile via the quotient rule (calculus-how-to-use-the-quotient-rule-to-differentiate-a-quotient-of-functions, n=0 -- the only zero-coverage skill in Calculus/Derivatives). The calculus track was written first per the concept sheet's own recommendation, but case-research found its load-bearing premise does not hold against real data (see redesign_2026_09_03). This case now ships as the linear track, the concept sheet's own documented fallback.

deliverables.text: Two cost equations, C_A(m) (built from Appendix A's fixed costs and Appendix B's per-mile rate) and C_B(m) (built from Appendix C's rideshare rate), presented together as a system of two linear equations in m and total cost C.
An algebraic solve of the D1 system (substitution or elimination, shown step by step) for the breakeven mileage m* where C_A(m*) = C_B(m*).

A comparison table evaluating C_A(m) and C_B(m) at m* (D2), the US average annual mileage (Appendix D), and Renata's own estimated mileage (Appendix D), stating which option wins and by how much at each point, plus a check of whether each option fits Renata's monthly transportation budget (Appendix D).
A graph plotting C_A(m) and C_B(m) as two lines on shared axes across at least 0 to the US average annual mileage (Appendix D), with m* and the D3 evaluation points labeled.

balance.argument_a: The fixed costs are real, but they're spread over comparably few miles once you account for how short Renata's actual route is -- and the per-mile cost of owning is roughly a sixth of the rideshare rate. Past the breakeven mileage m* (about 2,393.5 mi/yr), every additional mile costs six times less to own than to ride-share, and Renata's own estimated mileage (2,760 mi/yr) clears that bar, making Keys of Her Own about 11% cheaper for her specific situation.
balance.argument_b: Zero fixed-cost exposure: a light week costs almost nothing, and there's no loan or insurance bill sitting there whether or not she drives. Below m*, staying car-free is unambiguously cheaper, and the margin near m* is thin enough (11.24% at her own mileage estimate) that a meaningfully wrong mileage guess could flip the answer entirely -- unlike the fixed floor Option A carries no matter what.
balance.margin_basis: margin_pct = (C_B - C_A) / C_B, evaluated at MA1 (Renata's own estimated mileage, 2,760 mi/yr): C_A = 3039 + 0.2303(2760) = $3,674.63; C_B = 1.50(2760) = $4,140.00; margin = (4140 - 3674.63) / 4140 = 11.24%. Breakeven mileage m* = 3039 / (1.50 - 0.2303) = 3039 / 1.2697 ≈ 2,393.5 mi/yr, solved by setting C_A(m) = C_B(m). Both figures are final.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A compact, single-neighborhood home-health caseload: roughly 10 miles of driving per workday across her four-stop route (short legs, a few miles apart, no highway), 5 days/week for 50 weeks (250 workdays) = 2,500 mi/yr, plus about 260 mi/yr of weekend errands and other personal driving = 2,760 mi/yr total. Well below the FHWA national average (13,662 mi/yr, S4), which blends in long-haul commuters and rural drivers with very different routes.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The single most sensitive input in the case. Margin swings from 0% at m* (~2,393.5 mi/yr) to about 70% at the national average (13,662 mi/yr) for the same two cost equations -- revised down from the prior draft's 11,500 mi/yr (which produced a ~67% landslide, unbalanced per SPEC §2) specifically to land the margin at 11.24%, inside the concept sheet's 8-12% target. Disclosed openly as the intended discussion lever, not hidden.

modeling_assumptions.basis: BLS median annual pay for home health and personal care aides is $35,800 (May 2025, S5), ~$2,983/month gross. $350/month is ~12% of that, within the commonly cited 10-20% affordable-transportation share of gross income used in personal-finance guidance.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: At MA1's value (2,760 mi/yr), neither option exceeds this budget (C_A = $306/month, C_B = $345/month), so it does not currently bind either option -- D3 still requires the check. A tighter budget (e.g. $300/month) would rule out Option B specifically at this mileage; the connection between this cap and which option it could rule out is left for the Hero to discover.

derived.national_average_basis: At S4's 13,662 mi/yr: C_A = 3039 + 0.2303(13662) = $6,185.35; C_B = 1.50(13662) = $20,493.00; margin = (20493 - 6185.35) / 20493 = 69.8%. Used in FACILITATOR.md's landslide-at-national-average discussion and Socratic question 4.
derived.savings_at_MA1_basis: C_B - C_A at MA1 (2,760 mi/yr): 4140.00 - 3674.63 = $465.37/year, the dollar savings behind the 11.24% margin.
derived.miles_above_breakeven_at_MA1_basis: MA1 (2,760 mi/yr) minus m* (2,393.5 mi/yr) = 366.5 miles. Used in FACILITATOR.md Socratic question 3.
derived.annual_budget_cap_basis: MA2's $350/month cap x 12 = $4,200/year, the annual-equivalent of the monthly budget check in D3.
derived.socratic_q3_hypothetical_mileage_basis: An illustrative what-if mileage used only in FACILITATOR.md Socratic question 3 ('if her route actually adds up to, say, 3,500 miles a year') -- not a value used anywhere in case.md itself, recorded here so it is checkable rather than a silent guide-only figure.
derived.twist_low_basis: FACILITATOR.md's Twist re-solves at S3's corrected low-end metro rate ($0.90/mile, most US cities) instead of the $1.50/mile national average: C_B(2760) = 0.90 x 2760 = $2,484.00 against the unchanged C_A(2760) = $3,674.63; margin = (3674.63 - 2484.00) / 3674.63 = 32.4%, and the winner FLIPS to Option B (The All-App Life).
derived.twist_high_basis: FACILITATOR.md's Twist re-solves at S3's corrected high-end metro rate ($2.50/mile, highest-cost metros such as NYC) instead of the $1.50/mile national average: C_B(2760) = 2.50 x 2760 = $6,900.00 against the unchanged C_A(2760) = $3,674.63; margin = (6900.00 - 3674.63) / 6900.00 = 46.7%, and Option A (Keys of Her Own) wins even more comfortably.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1 is Renata's own FUTURE annual mileage -- an irreducible unknown at decision time, not a fact any amount of research could pin down in advance, since it depends on her route staying the same, her errand habits, and whether she picks up or drops visits. Tier 2 Probe 5 confirms the case's own documented fragility (case.json.modeling_assumptions[MA1].sensitivity, FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity note): a -50% flex (to 1,380 mi/yr) flips the verdict to Option B, margin 38.3%; a +50% flex (to 4,140 mi/yr) keeps Option A, margin 35.7%. This instability is the case's intended discussion lever, not an oversight -- MA1's own basis text already invites a Hero who thinks the real route is longer to re-run D2-D3, and FACILITATOR.md Socratic questions 1 and 3 exist specifically to surface it.

S3's $1.50/mile is a disclosed national average standing in for a real, sourced metro-by-metro range (corrected 2026-09-03 per Tier 2 Probe 6: $0.90/mile in most US cities up to $2.50+/mile in the highest-cost metros). Which end of that range applies to Renata's own specific, unnamed city is an irreducible unknown -- not a figure any further research on THIS case could resolve, since the case never names her city. FACILITATOR.md's Twist is built directly on this: at the low end ($0.90/mile) the verdict flips to Option B (margin 32.4%); at the high end ($2.50/mile) Option A wins by 46.7% (case.json.derived.twist_low_margin_pct / twist_high_margin_pct). This is an intended discussion lever, disclosed openly in the Twist rather than hidden, not a defect in the sourced $1.50/mile figure used for the case's own graded scenario.

sensitivity_note: This case touches personal financial precarity — a low-wage worker (home health aide) with no financial safety net making a decision she cannot afford to get wrong (SEE Background). Per SPEC §6, a one-line facilitator flag for the discussion lead: keep the discussion on the neutral, computable question (where the breakeven mileage falls, and where Renata's own mileage sits relative to it) rather than moralizing about her financial situation.
